title: Managing patients with acute, common single-system diseases in an inpatient setting
description: Work up and manage a common, single-system problem in a hospitalized neonate or infant, from evaluation through follow-up planning.
definingFunctions: Gather essential information through history, exam, and judicious labs and imaging.
Develop a prioritized differential that drives the right diagnostic tests.
Know and acquire the evidence for the primary problem, accounting for gestational age.
Build a plan covering the primary problem, level of care, discharge criteria, and follow-up.

levels.1: Observes the workup of single-system problems. Cannot yet gather a focused history and exam or frame a differential without the team interpreting the data.
levels.2: Gathers data and proposes a differential and plan with the attending guiding at the bedside, prompting on which labs and imaging are truly needed and reordering the diagnostic priorities.
levels.3a: Independently works up routine single-system problems with the attending in the unit, who confirms test selection, the working diagnosis, or the discharge and follow-up plan before it is enacted. Plans are reviewed with the attending in the moment rather than after they are enacted.
levels.3b: Manages common single-system cases start to finish, calling the attending for atypical presentations or when the course deviates from expected; plans are reviewed after the fact rather than beforehand.
levels.4: Independently gathers data, prioritizes the differential, applies gestational-age-appropriate evidence, and finalizes management, level of care, discharge criteria, and follow-up across the range of common problems.
levels.5: Performs independently and coaches junior learners on judicious testing, differential prioritization, and building a defensible discharge and follow-up plan.

title: Managing patients with complex diseases in the NICU
description: Manage infants with complex, multisystem disease in the NICU, including coordinating the team, managing uncertainty, and delivering difficult news.
definingFunctions: Build a multisystem plan addressing the primary problem, anticipated comorbidities, and case-management needs.
Coordinate care across the interdisciplinary team and reconcile disparate opinions.
Manage uncertainty as a team, with families, and personally.
Deliver bad news effectively and compassionately, tailored to the family.

levels.1: Observes the care of complex, multisystem patients. Cannot yet integrate multiple problems into a coherent plan or contribute to team coordination.
levels.2: Builds pieces of the plan with the attending structuring the multisystem assessment, naming anticipated comorbidities, and leading family and team communication.
levels.3a: Leads the plan for complex patients with the attending in the unit, who confirms the integration of comorbidities and case-management needs and joins high-stakes family conversations and bad-news delivery.
levels.3b: Manages stable complex patients and routine updates independently, reviewing prognostic uncertainty, difficult conversations, and bad-news delivery with the attending beforehand.
levels.4: Independently develops and adjusts the multisystem plan, reconciles disparate consultant opinions, manages uncertainty with team and family, and delivers bad news compassionately.
levels.5: Performs independently and mentors juniors on synthesizing multisystem plans, running interdisciplinary coordination, and leading difficult family conversations.

title: Collaborating with surgeons to manage patients with surgical problems in the NICU
description: Co-manage neonates with surgical problems across the perioperative course in partnership with surgery and anesthesia.
definingFunctions: Recognize surgical indications, the limits of medical management, and optimal timing of transfer.
Provide pre-, intra-, and postoperative stabilization, including nutrition, cardiopulmonary, and analgesic management.
Communicate directly with anesthesia and the surgical team.
Provide continuity so patients, families, and the team understand diagnosis, management, and follow-up.

levels.1: Observes surgical co-management. Cannot yet recognize when a problem has become surgical or anticipate perioperative needs.
levels.2: Participates in perioperative management with the attending directing recognition of surgical indications, stabilization, and communication with surgery and anesthesia.
levels.3a: Co-manages surgical patients with the attending immediately available, who confirms the timing of surgical involvement or transfer and the perioperative stabilization plan.
levels.3b: Manages routine perioperative courses and surgical communication independently, calling the attending when the indication, timing, or postoperative course is unclear.
levels.4: Independently recognizes surgical indications and their limits, times transfer appropriately, leads perioperative stabilization, and coordinates directly with surgery and anesthesia.
levels.5: Performs independently and teaches juniors to recognize surgical disease, anticipate perioperative needs, and communicate across teams.

title: Resuscitating and stabilizing neonates and infants tailored to severity of illness
description: Anticipate, lead, and debrief resuscitation and stabilization tailored to the infant's severity of illness.
definingFunctions: Anticipate and recognize infants requiring resuscitation and counsel at-risk parents before and after delivery.
Demonstrate effective resuscitation using guidelines appropriate to the patient and setting.
Act expeditiously, especially for airway management and vascular access.
Lead the team before, during, and after, including self-reflection and debriefs.

levels.1: Observes resuscitations. Cannot yet anticipate which deliveries are high-risk or sequence the resuscitation algorithm.
levels.2: Performs resuscitation with the attending calling each step and correcting technique on positive-pressure ventilation, rate, and escalation.
levels.3a: Leads routine resuscitation and stabilization with the attending at the warmer, who confirms airway placement, vascular access, and escalation decisions.
levels.3b: Independently leads and stabilizes for anticipated-risk deliveries, calling the attending for unexpected courses or failed airways; the case is reviewed afterward.
levels.4: Independently anticipates, leads, and stabilizes across gestational ages and acuity, prioritizes airway and access under time pressure, counsels families, and runs the debrief.
levels.5: Leads resuscitation while coaching junior team members through their roles and facilitates debriefs to improve future performance.

title: Managing neonatal care systems
description: Run the NICU as a system: triage, resource allocation, delegation, and communication under changing acuity.
definingFunctions: Assess a NICU system with changing acuity and census and anticipate sudden changes.
Prioritize distribution of resources (transport, beds, clinicians) to the highest-acuity needs.
Build a triage plan weighing patient needs, personnel, care environments, and family support.
Delegate appropriately, recognize limits, and communicate succinctly.

levels.1: Observes unit-level flow and triage. Cannot yet see the system beyond the individual patient.
levels.2: Contributes to triage and resource decisions with the attending actively directing prioritization, delegation, and communication.
levels.3a: Manages routine unit flow with the attending immediately available, who confirms triage priorities and resource allocation before major moves such as transfers, transport, or staffing changes.
levels.3b: Runs the unit for typical acuity independently, calling the attending when census surges, acuity spikes, or resources fall short.
levels.4: Independently assesses the system, anticipates sudden changes, prioritizes transport, beds, and clinicians, delegates appropriately, and communicates succinctly under pressure.
levels.5: Manages the system independently and develops junior learners' situational awareness, triage judgment, and delegation.

title: Executing clinical handovers within or across settings
description: Give and receive clinical handovers using a structured approach that prevents errors of omission.
definingFunctions: When handing over: review the record, use a structured tool, solicit questions, and convey preferences.
When receiving: summarize, ask questions to fill gaps, restate action items, and give feedback.
Use a structured, evidence-based approach or template.
Confirm shared understanding of contingencies and follow-up.

levels.1: Observes handovers. Handovers given are disorganized and omit key information; does not yet use a structured tool.
levels.2: Gives and receives handovers with the attending restructuring the content, prompting on omissions, and modeling closed-loop confirmation.
levels.3a: Runs structured handovers with the attending available, who spot-checks the written tool and confirms that action items and contingencies were conveyed.
levels.3b: Handles routine handovers independently using a consistent structure, escalating complex or high-risk transitions for review.
levels.4: Independently gives and receives handovers with a structured tool, conveys preferences and contingencies, and confirms shared understanding of action items.
levels.5: Performs independently and coaches juniors on structured handover technique, closed-loop communication, and giving feedback to the sender.

title: Promoting equitable care to address racism and other contributors to health inequities
description: Identify and act on drivers of inequity to provide equitable care at the individual and population level.
definingFunctions: Identify patients and populations at risk for poor outcomes and the systemic factors behind them.
Honor families' social identities and how they shape the experience of care.
Employ strategies to mitigate interpersonal and structural bias.
Advocate for patients and populations and tailor communication to health literacy and language.

levels.1: Observes equity-related aspects of care. Does not yet recognize social drivers of health or how bias shapes care in specific cases.
levels.2: Addresses equity considerations when the attending points them out, with coaching on identifying at-risk patients, using interpreters, and tailoring communication.
levels.3a: Identifies social drivers and adapts care for routine cases with the attending available to confirm the approach to complex situations such as advocacy or mitigating bias.
levels.3b: Independently identifies at-risk patients and tailors communication and resources, escalating complex advocacy or systemic barriers for input.
levels.4: Independently identifies social drivers, mitigates interpersonal and structural bias, advocates for patients and populations, and consistently tailors communication to health literacy and preferred language.
levels.5: Models equitable care and teaches juniors to recognize social drivers, name and mitigate bias, and advocate effectively.

title: Leading interprofessional teams to provide collaborative, family-centered care
description: Lead an interprofessional team to deliver collaborative, family-centered care.
definingFunctions: Engage team members, including families, in ways that respect and empower their roles.
Use evidence-based strategies to optimize team performance.
Supervise and teach to the needs of team members.
Seek and incorporate feedback with a commitment to improvement.

levels.1: Observes team leadership. Cannot yet engage the full interprofessional team or run collaborative decisions.
levels.2: Leads parts of the team with the attending modeling engagement, supervision, and how to fold family and staff input into the plan.
levels.3a: Leads the team for routine care with the attending available to confirm the approach to conflict, difficult dynamics, or complex family needs.
levels.3b: Runs the interprofessional team independently for stable situations, escalating conflict or high-stakes family decisions.
levels.4: Independently engages and supervises the team, uses evidence-based strategies for team performance, teaches to members' needs, and acts on feedback.
levels.5: Leads collaboratively and develops junior learners' team-leadership, supervision, and feedback skills.

title: Providing or requesting consultations
description: Provide or request consultations, matching involvement to the clinical question and communicating clearly.
definingFunctions: Determine when consultation is indicated and apply relevant expertise.
Recognize personal limits and scope to know when added expertise or referral is needed.
Synthesize essential information into a clear impression and evidence-informed plan.
Set the level of ongoing involvement and communicate findings to the referring team and family.

levels.1: Observes the consultation process. Cannot yet judge when a consult is warranted or frame a clear clinical question.
levels.2: Requests or provides consults with the attending shaping the clinical question, the impression, and the communication back to the referring team.
levels.3a: Handles routine consults with the attending available to confirm the impression, the recommendations, and the level of ongoing involvement.
levels.3b: Manages straightforward consults independently, escalating complex or high-urgency ones for review.
levels.4: Independently determines when consultation is indicated, synthesizes a clear impression and plan, sets appropriate ongoing involvement, and communicates clearly with the referring team and family.
levels.5: Performs independently and teaches juniors to frame consult questions, apply scope-of-practice judgment, and communicate recommendations.

title: Applying principles of scholarship to support practice and lifelong learning
description: Apply principles of scholarship to practice and lifelong learning across clinical, educational, QI, and advocacy work.
definingFunctions: Understand the foundations of scholarly inquiry (questions, methods, interpreting results).
Identify, appraise, and interpret scholarly work, attending to quality, bias, and applicability.
Recognize scholarly ethics: authorship, data integrity, conflicts of interest, responsible conduct.
Apply and communicate scholarship across clinical care, education, systems improvement, and advocacy.

levels.1: Observes scholarly activity. Cannot yet critically appraise literature or connect evidence to practice.
levels.2: Engages in appraisal and scholarly work with the attending guiding question framing, critical appraisal, and interpretation.
levels.3a: Appraises and applies evidence for routine questions with the attending available to confirm methodology, interpretation, and applicability.
levels.3b: Independently appraises and applies literature to practice, escalating methodologically complex questions or high-stakes interpretation.
levels.4: Independently formulates questions, appraises evidence for quality and bias, applies it across clinical, educational, QI, and advocacy settings, and upholds scholarly ethics.
levels.5: Performs independently and mentors juniors in critical appraisal, responsible conduct of scholarship, and communicating scholarly work.
